passages.text: A man has a right to be employed, to be trusted, to be loved, to be revered. The power of love, as the basis of a State, has never been tried.
passages.note: Feeling unvalued; the right to be trusted and loved

passages.text: Time, which shows so vacant, indivisible and divine in its coming, is slit and peddled into trifles and tatters. A door is to be painted, a lock to be repaired. I want wood or oil, or meal or salt; the house smokes, or I have a headache; then the tax, and an affair to be transacted with a man without heart or brains, and the stinging recollection of an injurious or very awkward word⁠—these eat up the hours. Do what we can, summer will have its flies; if we walk in the woods we must feed mosquitos; if we go a-fishing we must expect a wet coat.
passages.note: Days eaten by chores and petty annoyances

passages.text: Some wisdom comes out of every natural and innocent action. The domestic man, who loves no music so well as his kitchen clock and the airs which the logs sing to him as they burn on the hearth, has solaces which others never dream of.
passages.note: Simple domestic pleasures and quiet contentment

passages.text: Let a man keep the law⁠—any law⁠—and his way will be strown with satisfactions. There is more difference in the quality of our pleasures than in the amount.
passages.note: Discipline and the quality of pleasure
